# Digest slice 6 — Thielman Ephesians §IX–X (4:17–5:14)

## Coverage
Read lines 1–522 (full slice). Covers §IX.B "Living as Human Beings Newly Created in God's Image" (4:25–5:2) and all of §X "Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness" (5:3–14), including Additional Notes (textual criticism) for 4:28, 4:29, 4:32, 5:1, 5:2, 5:9, 5:14.

**NOTE on slice scope vs. brief:** The brief said this slice covers 4:17–5:14 and mentions the old-man/new-man material of 4:22–24. But the *exegesis* of 4:17–24 (the "no longer walk as Gentiles" / put-off-old-anthropos, put-on-new-anthropos section) is NOT in this slice — only the section-heading lines (1–5) and the introductory framing appear. The exegetical detail on 4:17–24 (palaios/kainos anthrōpos, apothesthai/endysasthai) must be in the PRIOR slice (slice 5). This slice's substantive exegesis begins at 4:25. I flag this so the integrator does not expect full 4:22–24 anthropology detail here — what is here is only cross-referential (Thielman repeatedly points *back* to 4:24's image-of-God/new-human-being theme as the motivation for 4:25–5:2).

**OVERFLOW:** Lines 506–522 run past the expected 5:14 endpoint into the introduction to §XI "Wise Conduct within the Household (5:15–6:9)" (5:15–6:9 overview: worship vs. pagan banqueting, household code preview). Extracted lightly below under Overflow.

## Claims — grouped by pericope

### 4:25–24 framing (the "therefore" / diό)
- **[4:25]** The section's "therefore" (διό) connects the admonitions not only to the whole put-off-old/put-on-new-human-being idea but "especially to the idea articulated in 4:24 that the newly donned human being is created in the image of God." Thielman's view: διό "points back primarily (although not solely) to 4:24, where the image-of-God theme is articulated as a motivation for ethics." (Thielman, following Lincoln 1990:300.) Voice: Thielman.
- **[4:25–5:2]** The admonitions are "practical illustrations of what it means to live as a new creature, made in God's image, and no longer under the sway of the old human being." Voice: Thielman.
- **Structure:** four admonitions (4:25, 28, 29, 31–32) follow a threefold pattern: negative command → positive counterpart → motivating reason. 4:26–27 and 4:30 break the pattern. Voice: Thielman.
- **[general]** "The combination of order and disorder... point both to the extemporary nature of the discourse and to its exemplary function." Voice: Thielman.

### 4:25 (truth-telling)
- **[4:25]** Negative uses aorist participle of ἀποτίθημι (apotithēmi, put off) — put off "falsehood" (τὸ ψεῦδος, to pseudos). "This language recalls the figure from 4:22 of putting off the clothing of the old human being that 'deceit' (ἀπάτη, apatē) was busily corrupting." — explicit link to old-anthropos of 4:22. Voice: Thielman.
- **[4:25]** May echo Rom. 1:25's τὸ ψεῦδος = Gentile idolatry exchanging truth about God for falsehood; "he may be thinking... also of the kind of theological falsehood... that filled Gentile religion... that eventually leads to the human disorientation and despair described in 4:17–19." Voice: Thielman (tentative).
- **[4:25]** Positive command "is so close to Zech. 8:16 LXX that there must be some connection" (only μετά for πρός differs). Positions on the connection: (a) O'Brien 1999:337–38 — "profound salvation-historical and typological" link, readers as fulfillment of new-Jerusalem promises; (b) Moritz 1996a / Sampley 1972 — author aware he was quoting OT; (c) others — author simply took over a traditional ethical sequence that had already absorbed Zech. 8:16 (parallels in T. Dan 4.7–5.2, T. Reu. 6.9, T. Benj. 10.3). Thielman's synthesis: "Paul probably found the reference to Zech. 8:16 in the tradition but... both recognized Zechariah as the source... and knew the broader context." Voice: reported positions + Thielman.
- **[4:25]** Motivation "we are members [μέλη, melē] of one another" recalls 4:15–16; Paul may have theological lying especially in view. Voice: Thielman.

### 4:26–27 (anger)
- **[4:26]** ὀργίζεσθε καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε quotes Ps. 4:5 LXX exactly. Voice: Thielman (primary-text observation).
- **[4:26]** Debate: some (Wallace 1989; 1996; Hoehner) read first imperative as genuine command implying anger sometimes appropriate/necessary. Thielman weighs against: context emphasizes the *second* (prohibition) imperative; "the first, positive imperative... is simply intended to set the stage for the prohibitions that follow." "Whether the anger is justified seems to be outside the purview of the admonition." Voice: reported + Thielman.
- **[4:26]** In antiquity ὀργίζομαι/ὀργή (orgē) "described the open and often-violent expression of what we call anger today" (W. V. Harris 2001:50–70). Voice: Thielman citing Harris.
- **[4:26]** παροργισμός (parorgismos, wrath) — rare term, LXX usually = "provocation of anger"; here synonym for ὀργή, prefix παρά hinting unattended anger increases. Proverbial wisdom (Plutarch; 1QS 5.26–6.1; CD; Micah 2:1). Voice: Thielman.
- **[4:27]** "to give place to" (διδόναι τόπον) = common Greek idiom for giving opportunity; devil as schemer (cf. 6:11) takes the opportunity of long-term anger. Voice: Thielman.

### 4:28 (theft)
- **[4:28]** κλέπτω/κλέπτης = stealing secretly, not violent robbery (Preisker, TDNT). Paul probably has in view the working poor of agrarian Roman Asia supplementing income by secret theft (Best 1997a). Not slaves, not wealthy. Voice: Thielman citing Best.
- **[4:28]** Best (1997a:181–83): the admonition reveals the social class of the first audience — included people poor enough to be tempted to steal and to be told to earn by manual labor. Voice: reported (Best), endorsed.
- **[4:28]** Purpose "that he might have something to share with the one who has need" — care for the needy "was one of the characteristic features of the early Christian movement" (cf. Acts 20:35; Titus 3:14; Did. 4.6). Voice: Thielman.

### 4:29 (speech)
- **[4:29]** σαπρός = literally "rotten/rancid"; figuratively "bad, evil, unwholesome." Could be sexually crude speech (Lincoln, Muddiman) but since opposite is "good for building up," probably any speech working against "the building up (οἰκοδομή) of the body of Christ" — "not merely 'ugly' but also 'useless.'" Voice: Thielman.
- **[4:29]** τῆς χρείας is difficult; Thielman (with parallel in T. Job 10.3) takes it as objective genitive: "edification where such edification is needed." Voice: Thielman.
- **[4:29]** "give grace (δῷ χάριν) to those who hear" — in Ephesians "give grace to" has specific theological meaning (3:2, 7, 8; 4:7): a gift enabling the recipient to accomplish God's task; here enabling needy people to function as God intended in the body of Christ. Voice: Thielman.

### 4:30 (grieve not the Holy Spirit) — see dedicated section below
- **[4:30]** μὴ λυπεῖτε τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τοῦ θεοῦ close to Isa. 63:9–10 (LXX has παροξύνω; Paul has λυπέω, closer to Hebrew עָצַב) — "Paul's word choice hints that he had the Isaiah passage in mind, perhaps in Hebrew" (Moritz 1996a:92). Voice: Thielman.
- **[4:30]** "sealed (ἐσφραγίσθητε) for the day of redemption (ἀπολυτρώσεως)" — clear echo of 1:13–14 opening benediction. "Day of redemption" = future day of wrath (5:6; 2:2) and of the people's deliverance/inheritance (1:14). Voice: Thielman.
- **[4:30]** Isa. 63:10 typology: as Israel grieved the Spirit of the God who redeemed them, so Paul's readers (God's redeemed people) can make the Spirit sad by unedifying conduct — "an admonition not to follow in the path of God's ancient people" (Schnackenburg 1991:209; O'Brien 1999:347–48; Thielman 2007:826). Paul does not make the Israel connection explicit (unlike 1 Cor. 10:1–13) but it "at least informs his own thinking." Voice: Thielman + reported.

### 4:31–32 (anger vices / kindness / forgiveness)
- **[4:31]** Five-vice list (πικρία bitterness, θυμός wrath, ὀργή anger/resentment, κραυγη yelling, βλασφημία slander). Some read these as five escalating stages of anger (Eadie, Schnackenburg; cf. Chrysippus SVF 3:395–97; Seneca; Ps.-Phocylides; Shepherd of Hermas Mand. 5.2.4). Thielman rejects: "Paul probably does not have such distinctions in mind"; all five can refer to angry verbal abuse; θυμός and ὀργή "probably synonymous here." "Paul's list... is an elaborate way of describing angry verbiage, not a taxonomy of anger." Voice: reported + Thielman.
- **[4:31]** κακία (kakia) = "a mean-spirited or vicious attitude" (BDAG) — inner attitude producing the verbal abuse. Voice: Thielman.
- **[4:31]** ἀρθήτω ("be removed") is aorist — sets it apart from the other ten present-tense imperatives in 4:25–32; underlines contrast between former unbeliever conduct and new life (Hoehner 2002:636). Voice: Thielman citing Hoehner.
- **[4:32]** χρηστοί (kind) recalls God's kindness (χρηστότης) shown to believers united with risen Christ (2:6–7); εὔσπλαγχνοι (compassionate) — God described so in Jewish theology (Pr. Man.). "Paul already hinted that he wanted his audience to imitate the character of the God whose graciousness to sinners he has described in 2:1–10." Voice: Thielman.
- **[4:32]** Forgive (χαρίζομαι) "just as God in Christ" forgave (χαρίζομαι); use of χαρίζομαι (vs. ἄφεσις in 1:7) may deliberately recall God's lavish grace (χάρις) in 2:5, 7, 8. Voice: Thielman.

### 5:1–2 (imitators of God; Christ's self-offering) — see 5:14 note-free; imitation theme
- **[5:1]** Thielman's view on οὖν: rejects both "new section start" (Hoehner) and mere link to previous (Lincoln) — prefers a "third, less popular interpretation": οὖν signals Paul "drawing his admonitions in 4:25–32 to a close by stating clearly the principle" — return to imitation-of-God (μιμηταί) theme. Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:1]** "the only reference in the Pauline literature to the imitation of God"; express command to "imitate God" never appears elsewhere in OT or NT. Imitation-of-God common in Hellenistic (esp. Platonic — Theaet. 176a–b ὁμοίωσις θεῷ; Philo) ethics, but Thielman: primary sources are Paul's own concept of the church as human being created in God's image (2:10, 15; 4:24) and the OT notion that Israel patterns its behavior on God's character (Lev. 11:44–45 "be holy for I am holy"; Deut. 10:17–19). Voice: Thielman + reported (Michaelis TDNT).
- **[5:1]** τέκνα ἀγαπητά (beloved children) alludes to readers' experience of adoption (1:5) and love (2:4; 3:17,19). Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:2]** περιπατέω "in love" — first use of περιπατέω since 4:17; positive counterpart to 4:17 "no longer walk as the Gentiles." Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:2]** παρέδωκεν ἑαυτὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν — atonement language going back to Jesus (Mark 10:45; 1 Cor 11:24), rooted in Isa. 53 LXX (paradidonai 3× for the servant; Hengel 1981:36). Reflexive "he gave himself" + "offering (προσφοράν) and sacrifice (θυσίαν)... fragrant aroma (ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας)" emphasize Christ's *own willingness*, arising from love, to atone. "Fragrant aroma" = OT idiom for God's acceptance of a sincere sacrifice. Voice: Thielman.

### 5:3–7 (sexual immorality and greed)
- **[§X intro]** Section governed by shame-vs-fitting and darkness-vs-light contrasts, not the put-on/put-off and imitation themes of the prior section. "Trio of sinful trios" (three vices, three speech-sins, three types of person, 5:3–5) counterbalanced by "thanksgiving" (5:4) and a trio of virtues (5:9). Voice: Thielman.
- **[§X intro]** Thielman's disputed reading of the passage's target: NOT primarily church discipline / false teachers (against Best, Hoehner); rather "a complex mixture" — avoid immorality/greed AND work for the transformation of *unbelievers* mired in these sins. "Sons of disobedience" (5:6) = unbelieving Gentiles (as in 2:2); "them" (5:12) = unbelievers; the 5:14 hymn calls unbelievers (dead in trespasses, 2:1) to rise. Voice: Thielman (against Best/Hoehner).
- **[5:3]** πορνεία, ἀκαθαρσία πᾶσα (uncleanness) vs. πλεονεξία (pleonexia, greed). Rejects the venerable Origen/Jerome reading that "greed" = *sexual* greed (coveting another's wife); the conjunction ἤ (or) separates the two sexual vices from greed — "he is viewing sexual immorality and greed separately, as two distinct vices." Voice: Thielman (against Origen/Jerome).
- **[5:3]** πορνεία = characteristically Gentile vice, often connected with idolatry (Wis. 14:12; T. Reu. 4.6; 1 Cor. 10:7–8). Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:3]** πλεονεξία generally = acquiring/holding wealth. Rosner 2007: greed among earliest Christians = "unwillingness to share one's possessions with the needy." Paul may say to the wealthy what he said to the working poor in 4:28. Voice: Thielman citing Rosner.
- **[5:3]** "not even be named (ὀνομαζέσθω)" = emphatic (not pedantic contradiction); a "holy" (ἅγιος) culture utterly different from 4:17–19. Parallel: Dio Chrysostom on civil strife. Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:4]** Three rare speech-vices (only here in Greek Bible): αἰσχρότης (obscenity — connotes unnatural/disordered sexual behavior/talk), μωρολογία (nonsensical talk, associated with drunkenness/banqueting per Plutarch), εὐτραπελία (clever wit — an admirable talent abused into malicious/sexually vulgar humor; Hultin 2008). Banquet/symposium setting. Voice: Thielman citing Hultin, Plutarch, Josephus.
- **[5:4]** Instead: "thanksgiving" (εὐχαριστία) — distinctively Pauline word (12 of 15 NT uses Pauline), always directed to God; contrasts with drunkenness (5:18–20). Voice: Thielman citing Best/Hoehner.
- **[5:5]** ἴστε γινώσκοντες — probably "Be sure you understand this." Three types of person: πόρνος, ἀκάθαρτος, πλεονέκτης, with no inheritance (κληρονομία) "in the kingdom of the Messiah and of God." Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:5]** GREED = IDOLATRY: "the greedy person is an εἰδωλολάτρης (eidōlolatrēs, idolater)." Same equation in Col. 3:5 (πλεονεξία = εἰδωλολατρία). Per Rosner 2007:159–64: "idolater/idolatry" used *metaphorically* — giving to money the love/devotion/trust/service/obedience owed to God alone; "not simply that 'love of money leads to idolatry'... but that it is, metaphorically speaking, idolatry." Ancient parallels: Job 31:24–28; Philo Spec. Laws 1.23; Matt. 6:24; Polycarp Phil. 11.2. Voice: Thielman citing Rosner (heavily endorsed).
- **[5:5]** Ephesians uniquely uses *present* tense (οὐκ ἔχει) for the inheritance and the unique phrase "kingdom of the Messiah and of God" (ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ θεοῦ) — emphasizing the *present* reign of Messiah + God (allusions to Ps. 110:1 / Ps. 8:7 via 1:20, 22; believers seated with Christ, 2:6). Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:6–7]** "empty words" = probably false teaching (cf. 4:14) claiming no judgment for immorality/greed (parallels 2 Pet., Jude). God's wrath "is coming" (ἔρχεται) — Thielman argues for *future* reference (against present-outpouring readings of Calvin, Best); the Spirit-seal protects against coming wrath (1:13). "Sons of disobedience" = unbelievers (2:2). συμμέτοχοι (5:7) = fullest participation; only other NT use 3:6 (Gentiles' full participation in God's people). Voice: Thielman.

### 5:8–14 (light and darkness; transformation)
- **[5:8]** "you were once (ποτέ) darkness, but now (νῦν δέ) are light in the Lord" — not merely *in* darkness/light but *are* darkness/light; existence defined by the Lord. ποτέ/νῦν δέ = conversion + ethical-instruction formula characteristic of Ephesians (2:11, 13). Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:8]** Light/darkness ethical use parallels 1 Thess. 5:4–11 and Rom. 13:11–14 (both link eschatology + ethics, both mingle put-off/put-on and armor imagery — cf. Eph 4:22–24; 6:10–17). KEY DIFFERENCE: Ephesians is more "realized" — ethics based on present existence *as* light, not on the soon-coming day; after 5:6 the "final day disappears from view." "the difference is one of emphasis rather than contradiction." Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:9]** Parenthesis: "fruit of the light" (τοῦ φωτός; textual variant τοῦ πνεύματος from Gal 5:22 — see Additional Note) = "all goodness (ἀγαθωσύνη) and righteousness (δικαιοσύνη) and truth (ἀλήθεια)" — trio of virtues contrasting the vice-trios. ἀγαθωσύνη = practical benevolence/doing good (opposite of the greed of 5:3–5); δικαιοσύνη here = "upright behavior" (not forensic); ἀλήθεια here = ethical honesty. The three describe God's character → imitation-of-God theme (4:24; 5:1). Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:10]** δοκιμάζοντες = "finding out/exercise of critical judgment" what pleases the Lord. Thielman: Paul's ethics deliberately leave room for believers' renewed thinking (Rom. 12:2; 14:5, 22; 15:14; Philemon appeal). Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:11]** συγκοινωνεῖτε (don't participate) in "unfruitful (ἀκάρποις) works of darkness" — repeats 5:7 (συμμέτοχοι); both σύν-compounds highlight incompatibility with the σύν-community of God's people (2:5,6,19,21–22). Darkness produces activity but "unfruitful" — yields no profit, part of the futility theme (2:1–3; 4:17–19). Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:11]** ἐλέγχειν (expose) — long semantic survey (uncover / expose evil / rebuke / correct-to-restore / lead to conversion, e.g. 1 Cor. 14:24–25). Thielman: object is "the unfruitful works of darkness" (the *deeds*, not the people); emphasis on stripping the attractive veneer off immorality and greed. "It is the deeds... that are exposed as evil, not the people who practice them." Voice: Thielman.
- **[5:12]** "shameful even to talk about" = exaggeration for emphasis (against those who infer exposure must be wordless — John of Damascus, Barth, Lincoln). "them" (ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν) = "the sons of disobedience" = unbelievers (against Best/Hoehner who read errant believers). Done "in secret" (κρυφῇ) — because doers ashamed or society viewed acts with disgust; some unbelieving Gentiles had sensitive consciences (Rom. 2:15–16; 1 Cor. 5:1). Voice: Thielman (against Best/Hoehner).
- **[5:13]** ὑπὸ τοῦ φωτός ("by the light") attaches to ἐλεγχόμενα (being exposed), not to φανεροῦται — against Lincoln, who prefers attaching it forward to ease the shift from light=believers to light=Christ. Everything exposed by the light (= believers) becomes visible; via 1 Cor. 14:24–25, what becomes visible = the inconsistency between unbelievers' conduct and convictions. Voice: Thielman (against Lincoln).
- **[5:14a]** "everything visible is light" — rejects the middle-voice reading "whatever makes manifest is light" (Abbott, Eadie): φανερόω never middle in 48 NT uses. Via 1 Cor. 14:24–25 + 2 Cor. 4:6 + Eph 5:8 = about *conversion*: all made visible by the light is itself transformed into light; "light" = metaphor for the believer (as in 5:8). Voice: Thielman.

## Old/new anthropos (4:22–24) — detail present in THIS slice
The full exegesis of 4:22–24 is NOT in this slice (see Coverage note; it is in slice 5). What IS here is repeated *back-reference* used to frame the ethics of 4:25–5:2:
- Thielman treats the pivot of the whole section as 4:24: "the newly donned human being is created in the image of God" — the διό of 4:25 points "primarily (although not solely) to 4:24, where the image-of-God theme is articulated as a motivation for ethics." (Line 40)
- 4:25's "put off (ἀποτίθημι) falsehood" "recalls the figure from 4:22 of putting off the clothing of the old human being that 'deceit' (ἀπάτη, apatē) was busily corrupting, and provides a concrete example of how the old human being manifests itself in day-to-day life." (Line 44) — explicit clothing/put-off link between the 4:22 palaios anthrōpos and the concrete vice of lying.
- The imitation-of-God theme (5:1) is grounded by Thielman in "Paul's own concept of the church as a human being created in God's image (2:10, 15; 4:24; cf. Gal. 6:15; 2 Cor. 5:17)" — explicitly tying the 4:24 "new human being" to the corporate "one new human being" ecclesiology of 2:15 ("in this letter Paul has already developed the idea that his readers, as objects of God's mercy and grace, form a new human creation (2:10, 15)"). (Lines 172, 204–206)
- The 5:9 virtue-trio (goodness/righteousness/truth) "appear together in 4:24" (dikaiosynē + alētheia) — Thielman notes "Behind Paul's choice of these three terms... is probably the theme of the imitation of God that has surfaced more explicitly in 4:24 and 5:1." Links new-creation-in-God's-image (4:24) → ethical virtues. (Lines 397, 399)
- NB for concept **heis-kainos-anthropos**: this slice does NOT give the exegesis of the term kainos anthrōpos itself; it gives the *ethical outworking* and repeatedly ties the individual "new human being" of 4:24 to the corporate new humanity of 2:10, 15. The put-off/put-on (apotithēmi/endyō) clothing imagery appears via the 4:22 back-reference and via the 1 Thess/Rom parallels (line 383: "the darkness-light metaphor mingles with the metaphor of 'putting off' certain behaviors and 'putting on' other attitudes... cf. Eph. 4:22–24").

## The 5:14 citation ("Awake, O sleeper") — full detail on origin
Text (Thielman's rendering, lines 351–355):
> Get up, O sleeper, / And rise from the dead, / And Christ will shine on you.

- **Introductory formula** διὸ λέγει ("therefore it says") indicates Paul thought it "carried the authority of Scripture." διὸ λέγει occurs 3× NT (here, 4:8, James 4:6); λέγει ("it says") occurs 35× in Pauline corpus, all but 3 connected with the speech of Scripture. "Scripture continues to 'speak' in the present because it remains authoritative." (Lines 449, 463)
- **Form:** Thielman judges it "a piece of poetry... if we measure it by Hebrew rather than Greek standards" — verbs begin each line (un-Greek; typical of Jewish/early-Christian liturgy per Norden 1923:257–58); cannot be scanned by Greek meter (Noack 1952); parallelism reminiscent of Hebrew poetry. (Line 447)
- **Two governing questions:** (1) where it originated; (2) why Paul cited it as Scripture. (Line 449)
- **Rejected theory A — paraphrase of an OT text:** candidates Isa. 60:1 (most common), Isa. 26:19, Isa. 26:19 + 9:2, Jon. 1:6. Thielman rejects: the very variety of proposals shows the theory's weakness; verbal parallels "not close"; all candidates describe transformation of a *corporate* entity (God's people), whereas 5:14b addresses an *individual* (2nd-sing imperatives); and (Abbott 1897) the mention of *Christ* "is fatal to the idea of a quotation" from the OT. (Lines 451–453)
- **Rejected theory B — a lost/unknown OT prophecy** (Elijah, Jeremiah, or Enoch, entertained then rejected by Jerome): the variety of proposed names again counts against it — ancient interpreters were "casting around for an authoritative name" for material they correctly sensed Paul quoted authoritatively. (Line 455)
- **Rejected theory C — pagan/Gnostic/mystery origin:** Reitzenstein (early alchemistic writing), Bultmann ("cast in quite Gnostic terms"), Strecker (Gnostic + mystery-cult influence). Thielman rejects: wake-from-sleep/resurrection/enlightenment imagery was pervasive in the *Jewish* religious atmosphere (1QHa 11.19–22; Jos. Asen. 8.10–11; Pss. Sol. 16.1–4) and describes conversion/joining the covenant community. (Lines 457–459)
- **THIELMAN'S OWN VIEW:** "Although the quotation is not directly from the OT, then, it was probably composed within early Jewish Christianity." Grounds: poetic structure, use of metaphor, reference to "Christ" (ὁ Χριστός, "the Messiah"), and its occurrence within Ephesians (a text deeply indebted to the OT). It is "a carefully crafted piece of early Jewish-Christian liturgy that was probably widely used in the first century but... later detached from its original context or completely lost." Paul assumes his audience will recognize it (so not spontaneous Spirit-speech of 1 Cor. 14:26). Possible original settings Paul leaves unresolved: a Spirit-inspired psalm, a baptismal-liturgy fragment, or a hymn anticipating Christ's return/resurrection. (Lines 461, 465–467)
- **Function/meaning:** the quotation "appears to envision a preacher of the gospel calling the unbeliever, who is imagined as asleep and dead, to a resurrected life in which the light of Christ 'will shine' (ἐπιφαύσει)." Lines 1–2 recall 2:1, 5–6 (dead in trespasses → made alive/raised/seated); line 3 recalls 5:8 (darkness → light). It is Paul's proof that "everything illuminated is light" = a description of *conversion*. (Lines 469–471)
- **Contrast with 1 Thess. 5 / Rom. 13:** despite close language, there sleep/wake imagery admonishes *believers* to be ready for the day of the Lord; here it urges the *unbeliever* to recognize the day of the Lord has "in a sense, already come." (Line 475)
- **Textual variant (Additional Note 5:14):** "perhaps the strangest textual variant in Ephesians" — Western witnesses (D, Old Latin, Ambrosiaster, etc.) read ἐπιψαύσεις τοῦ Χριστοῦ / ἐπιψαύσει... ("you will touch Christ" / "Christ will touch you") instead of ἐπιφαύσει σοι ὁ Χριστός ("Christ will shine on you"). Chrysostom and Jerome knew and rejected it; correct reading is ἐπιφαύσει ("shine"). The "touch" variant probably arose from the legend that Adam's skull lay buried at Golgotha (Christ's blood "touched" the buried Adam) — Jerome heard a preacher use it as a "theatrical marvel" that drew applause; same legend+text link in Epiphanius (Pan. 46.5.8–9, but with accurate text). (Lines 489–491)

## Overflow (lines 506–522) — intro to §XI (5:15–6:9), beyond expected endpoint
- Up to 5:14 Paul admonished "mainly through contrast" (how you once lived / how pagans live vs. new life). After transitional 5:15–18, Paul turns to a wholly positive description of Christian corporate worship (5:19–20) and household life (5:21–6:9) = "the life of wisdom lived within the sphere of the Spirit." Voice: Thielman.
- Implied contrast: Christian corporate worship vs. pagan corporate banqueting; the Christian home vs. surrounding sexual immorality. Thielman notes no neat separation existed — ancient banqueting was notorious for sexual immorality (bawdy songs/jokes), and Christian worship also took place in wealthy households and included a meal (1 Cor. 11; Jude 12; 2 Pet. 2:13); some "Christians" defended immoral banqueting with "specious theological arguments." Paul interested in clear separation from the symposia/convivia/drinking parties of the wealthy. Voice: Thielman.
- Household code preview: 5:21–6:9 organized by three ancient household relationships — wife/husband (5:21–33), children/parents (6:1–4), slaves/masters (6:5–9), unified by "wise conduct within the household." Voice: Thielman.

## Named scholars/positions cited
- **O'Brien 1999** — strong salvation-historical/typological reading of Zech. 8 in 4:25 (Thielman partly agrees, partly qualifies); Isa. 63:10 Israel typology in 4:30.
- **Lincoln 1990** — διό→4:24; σαπρός as sexual; 5:13 ὑπὸ τοῦ φωτός forward-attachment (Thielman disagrees); pronoun textual matters.
- **Best 1997a / 1998** — social class of audience from 4:28 (endorsed); 5:6 deceivers as internal false teachers, 5:11–12 exposed deeds as errant believers, secret conduct (Thielman DISAGREES on the unbeliever question).
- **Hoehner 2002** — aorist ἀρθήτω (4:31); anger reading; church-discipline reading of 5:11–13 (Thielman disagrees); ἴστε γινώσκοντες.
- **Rosner 2007** — greed as idolatry (heavily endorsed for 5:3, 5).
- **W. V. Harris 2001** — terminology of anger in classical antiquity (4:26, 4:31).
- **Wallace 1989/1996** — "be angry" as genuine command (Thielman weighs against).
- **Schnackenburg 1991** — Isa. 63:10 typology; five-stage anger reading; two-section structure of 5:3–14.
- **Moritz 1996a** — Zech. 8:16 awareness; Isa. 63 in Hebrew behind 4:30.
- **Sampley 1972** — structural parallel Eph 4:25–30 // Zech 8:16–17.
- **Hengel 1981** — Isa. 53 LXX behind Christ's self-giving (5:2).
- **Hultin 2008** — εὐτραπελία as admirable-but-abusable wit (5:4).
- **Michaelis, TDNT** — imitation-of-God tradition (Plato, Philo) for 5:1.
- **Abbott 1897** — "Christ mention fatal to OT-quotation idea"; middle-voice reading of 5:14a (Thielman rejects); Adam's-skull legend.
- **Norden 1923 / Noack 1952** — form of 5:14 as Hebrew-style liturgical poetry.
- **Reitzenstein / Bultmann / Strecker / Conzelmann** — Gnostic/mystery-cult origin theories for 5:14 (Thielman rejects).
- **Kuhn 1968; Berger 1995** — Jewish conversion/awakening parallels (1QHa, Jos. Asen., Pss. Sol.).
- **Metzger 1994** — textual notes (4:32, 5:9, 5:14).
- **Jerome / Chrysostom / Epiphanius / Theodoret** — patristic witnesses to the 5:14 "touch" variant and Adam-skull legend.
- **Origen / Jerome** — venerable reading of πλεονεξία as sexual greed (5:3; Thielman rejects).

## Notable Greek terms with glosses
- **παλαιὸς ἄνθρωπος / καινὸς ἄνθρωπος** — old/new human being (referenced back to 4:22–24; exegesis in prior slice, but framing throughout: 4:25, 5:1, 5:9 tied to 4:24 image-of-God).
- **ἀποτίθημι (apotithēmi)** — put off; aorist participle at 4:25 "put off falsehood" (clothing imagery from 4:22).
- **τὸ ψεῦδος (to pseudos)** — falsehood/a lie (4:25; cf. Rom. 1:25).
- **ἀπάτη (apatē)** — deceit, corrupting the old human being (4:22, cited at 4:25).
- **παροργισμός (parorgismos)** — wrath/provocation of anger (4:26).
- **τόπον τῷ διαβόλῳ** — "place to the devil" (4:27).
- **σαπρός (sapros)** — rotten/rancid; here useless & ugly speech (4:29).
- **οἰκοδομή (oikodomē)** — building up/edification (4:29).
- **χάριν δοῦναι** — give grace (4:29); in Ephesians = task-enabling gift.
- **λυπέω (lypeō)** — grieve/vex (4:30; vs. LXX παροξύνω, matching Hebrew עָצַב).
- **ἐσφραγίσθητε (esphragisthēte)** — you were sealed (4:30; cf. 1:13).
- **ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrōsis)** — redemption; "day of redemption" (4:30).
- **πικρία, θυμός, ὀργή, κραυγή, βλασφημία, κακία** — bitterness, wrath, anger, yelling, slander, mean-spiritedness (4:31).
- **χρηστοί / εὔσπλαγχνοι / χαρίζομαι** — kind / compassionate / forgive-graciously (4:32).
- **μιμηταί (mimētai)** — imitators (of God) (5:1); ὁμοίωσις θεῷ (Plato, becoming like God).
- **περιπατέω (peripateō)** — walk (5:2; cf. 4:17).
- **προσφορά / θυσία / ὀσμὴ εὐωδίας** — offering / sacrifice / fragrant aroma (5:2).
- **πορνεία (porneia)** — sexual immorality (5:3).
- **ἀκαθαρσία (akatharsia)** — uncleanness/sexual deviance (5:3).
- **πλεονεξία / πλεονέκτης (pleonexia / pleonektēs)** — greed / greedy person (5:3, 5).
- **εἰδωλολάτρης / εἰδωλολατρία (eidōlolatrēs / eidōlolatria)** — idolater / idolatry (5:5; greed=idolatry, metaphorical).
- **αἰσχρότης / μωρολογία / εὐτραπελία** — obscenity / nonsensical talk / (abused) clever wit (5:4).
- **εὐχαριστία (eucharistia)** — thanksgiving (5:4).
- **βασιλεία τοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ θεοῦ** — kingdom of the Messiah and of God (5:5, unique phrase).
- **συμμέτοχοι / συγκοινωνεῖτε** — sharers-together / participate-with (5:7, 11).
- **σκότος / φῶς (skotos / phōs)** — darkness / light (5:8ff).
- **τέκνα φωτός** — children of the light (5:8).
- **ἀγαθωσύνη / δικαιοσύνη / ἀλήθεια** — goodness / righteousness / truth (5:9, fruit of the light).
- **δοκιμάζω (dokimazō)** — exercise critical judgment / find out (5:10).
- **ἄκαρπος (akarpos)** — unfruitful (5:11).
- **ἐλέγχω (elenchō)** — expose / reprove / convict (5:11, 13).
- **φανερόω (phaneroō)** — make visible/manifest (5:13, 14a).
- **ἐπιφαύσει (epiphausei)** — "(Christ) will shine" (5:14b; variant ἐπιψαύσει "will touch").
- **ὁ Χριστός (ho Christos)** — "the Messiah/Christ" (5:14b; the presence of this name is Thielman's key argument the citation is not OT).
